Overnight severe weather persisted into the early morning hours of April 27, and would continue virtually unbroken for the remainder of the day. At 06:10 UTC, the SPC issued a second-consecutive, high risk day-one outlook, featuring a 30% hatched risk of tornadoes centered over northern Alabama.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-43) At 16:30 UTC (11:30 AM CDT) this region was expanded to include portions of eastern Mississippi, southern Tennessee, and northwest Georgia. Additionally, an exceedingly rare, 45% hatched risk of tornadoes was introduced along a corridor from [Meridian, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meridian,_Mississippi "Meridian, Mississippi"), to [Huntsville, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huntsville,_Alabama "Huntsville, Alabama"). Environmental conditions continued to be extremely favorable for discrete tornadic supercells throughout the day.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-April27-25)

#### Morning squall lines

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2011_Super_Outbreak&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Morning squall lines")]

During the early morning, a cold front with several embedded low pressure areas extended from east [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas") northeastward into the [Ohio River Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River_Valley "Ohio River Valley"). An upper-level disturbance that had moved across the frontal boundary the previous evening sparked an area of thunderstorms that morphed into a [squall line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squall_line "Squall line"). This line of severe thunderstorms would produce tornadic activity from the evening on April 26 into the late morning of April 27. Early in the morning the squall line, packing straight-line winds and numerous embedded tornadoes, moved through [Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana "Louisiana") and [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi") before proceeding to affect [North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Alabama "North Alabama") and [Central Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Alabama "Central Alabama") and parts of [Middle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Tennessee "Middle Tennessee") and [East Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Tennessee "East Tennessee"). The line strengthened as it moved through [Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama "Alabama"), partially due to a high amount of low-level moisture from the [Gulf of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico") and increasing [wind shear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_shear "Wind shear").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-April_27_Conditions_HUN-44)

A majority of the tornadoes embedded in this initial squall line were weak, though several were strong and as such caused significant damage. An EF3 tornado caused major damage to homes in [Coaling, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coaling,_Alabama "Coaling, Alabama"), an EF2 and an EF3 tornado produced severe damage and a fatality near [Eupora, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eupora,_Mississippi "Eupora, Mississippi"). Another EF3 tornado resulted in heavy damage in downtown [Cordova, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordova,_Alabama "Cordova, Alabama"), which was struck by a violent EF4 tornado later that afternoon. An EF2 also struck [Cahaba Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahaba_Heights "Cahaba Heights") near [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham,_Alabama "Birmingham, Alabama"). One embedded cell began producing tornadoes just after 5:00 a.m. CDT (10:00 UTC), starting with an EF1 tornado striking [Berry, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berry,_Alabama "Berry, Alabama"). This was soon followed by the Cordova EF3 tornado.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-2011-super-outbreak-45) As the line entered [Cullman County, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cullman_County,_Alabama "Cullman County, Alabama"), the cell, a [mesoscale convective vortex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoscale_convective_vortex "Mesoscale convective vortex") (MCV), began exhibiting a comma head appearance and produced another long-tracked EF2 tornado that struck the town of [Hanceville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanceville,_Alabama "Hanceville, Alabama"), killing one person. The MCV would then produce 13 tornadoes (most rated EF1) to the northeast in [Marshall County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_County,_Alabama "Marshall County, Alabama"), many of which occurred simultaneously. Two more tornadoes were produced as the comma head-shaped embedded cell continued northeast along the [Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_County,_Alabama "Jackson County, Alabama")/[DeKalb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DeKalb_County,_Alabama "DeKalb County, Alabama") county line, including a long-track EF1 that resulted in a fatality near [Pisgah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pisgah,_Alabama "Pisgah, Alabama"). The same area was impacted later that day by a [high-end EF4 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#Pisgah%E2%80%93Flat_Rock%E2%80%93Higdon,_Alabama/Trenton,_Georgia).[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-April_27_Conditions_HUN-44) Another EF1 tornado occurred in [Dade County, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dade_County,_Georgia "Dade County, Georgia"), with the cell, and six more tornadoes struck [Hamilton County, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton_County,_Tennessee "Hamilton County, Tennessee"), five of which were in the [Chattanooga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chattanooga,_Tennessee "Chattanooga, Tennessee") area. The 26th and final tornado produced by the MCV was an EF2 tornado in northern [Bradley County, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradley_County,_Tennessee "Bradley County, Tennessee"), which hit at 9:45 a.m. EDT (13:45 UTC).[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-MRXApril27-46) The initial storms caused widespread [power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_line "Power line") and [telephone line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telephone_line "Telephone line") outages across Alabama and Tennessee. This line of storms also caused some [NOAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Oceanic_and_Atmospheric_Administration "National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration")[weather radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NOAA_Weather_Radio "NOAA Weather Radio") transmitter sites to stop functioning for the remainder of the outbreak. Because of this, more than one million customers were without power and had no warning of any approaching tornadoes later that day.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-April_27_Conditions_HUN-44)

From the late morning to the early afternoon, another squall line moved through northern parts of Mississippi and Alabama as high wind shear and low-level moisture persisted. However, this time several discrete [supercells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell "Supercell") developed along and in front of the line, spawning seven weak tornadoes across [Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_County,_Alabama "Morgan County, Alabama"), [Limestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limestone_County,_Alabama "Limestone County, Alabama"), and [Madison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_County,_Alabama "Madison County, Alabama") Counties in northern Alabama around noon that day.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-April_27_Conditions_HUN-44)

#### Afternoon supercells

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2011_Super_Outbreak&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Afternoon supercells")]

[![Image 371: Brown dirt area and a green field are seen under a clear blue sky](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/Philadelphia%2C_MS_ground_scouring.jpg/250px-Philadelphia%2C_MS_ground_scouring.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Philadelphia,_MS_ground_scouring.jpg)

Extremely deep ground scouring near [Philadelphia, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia,_Mississippi "Philadelphia, Mississippi"), caused by a fast-moving EF5 tornado that killed three people.

The most intense supercells of the outbreak developed around midday in central Mississippi and began tracking eastward. With the extreme instability and wind shear, they quickly intensified and eventually became tornadic, shortly thereafter resulting in strong to violent tornadoes. Responding to the high risk issued by the SPC and the already unstable atmosphere expected to become even more unstable throughout the afternoon, a [PDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particularly_dangerous_situation "Particularly dangerous situation")[tornado watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_watch "Tornado watch") was issued at 1:45 p.m. CDT (18:45 UTC) for much of Alabama and portions of Mississippi, Tennessee, and Georgia. A widespread complex of supercell storms overspread the states of Mississippi and Alabama and violent tornadoes began rapidly touching down as the afternoon progressed.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-April_27_Conditions_HUN-44)

By mid-afternoon, as wind shear and low-level moisture continued to dramatically increase, a [tornado emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_emergency "Tornado emergency") was declared for [Neshoba County, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neshoba_County,_Mississippi "Neshoba County, Mississippi"), as a large tornado was reported on the ground by both storm spotters and a camera atop a television tower from [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company "American Broadcasting Company") affiliate [WTOK-TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WTOK-TV "WTOK-TV") (channel 11) in [Meridian, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meridian,_Mississippi "Meridian, Mississippi"). This powerful EF5 tornado caused incredible damage northeast of [Philadelphia, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia,_Mississippi "Philadelphia, Mississippi"), where pavement was torn off from roads, vehicles were thrown, and the ground was scoured out to a depth of 2 feet (0.61 m) by the tornado. Three people died when a mobile home was thrown 300 yards (270 m) into a wooded area, obliterating it in the process.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-47) Another very long-tracked EF4 tornado passed near the town of [Enterprise, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enterprise,_Clarke_County,_Mississippi "Enterprise, Clarke County, Mississippi"), killing seven people before crossing into Alabama and eventually dissipating. Four tornadoes were officially rated EF5 on the [Enhanced Fujita scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced_Fujita_scale "Enhanced Fujita scale") that day. One of those EF5 tornadoes struck the town of [Smithville, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithville,_Mississippi "Smithville, Mississippi"), where many well-built brick homes were reduced to bare slabs, numerous hardwood trees were completely debarked, and an SUV was hurled half a mile into the top of the town's water tower, subsequently leaving behind a visible dent. Another long-tracked EF5 wedge tornado passed through rural portions of Alabama and Tennessee, becoming the deadliest tornado of the outbreak as it completely devastated the towns of [Hackleburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hackleburg,_Alabama "Hackleburg, Alabama"), [Phil Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Campbell,_Alabama "Phil Campbell, Alabama"), [Mount Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Hope,_Lawrence_County,_Alabama "Mount Hope, Lawrence County, Alabama"), [Tanner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanner,_Alabama "Tanner, Alabama"), and [Harvest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvest,_Alabama "Harvest, Alabama"), killing 72 people. This marks only the second day in history (after [April 3, 1974](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_Super_Outbreak "1974 Super Outbreak")) that there were more than two F5/EF5 tornadoes reported.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-48)

The tornadoes continued tracking through central Alabama that afternoon and into the early evening. A dangerous and destructive tornado struck the city of [Cullman, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cullman,_Alabama "Cullman, Alabama"), at around 3:00 p.m. CDT (20:00 UTC). This large, multiple-vortex tornado was captured on several tower cameras from [television stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_station "Television station"), such as [Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_Broadcasting_Company "Fox Broadcasting Company") affiliate [WBRC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WBRC "WBRC") (channel 6) and ABC affiliate [WBMA-LD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WBMA-LD "WBMA-LD")/[WCFT-TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSES "WSES")/[WJSU-TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WGWW "WGWW") (channels 58, 33, and 40) both out of [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham,_Alabama "Birmingham, Alabama"). The tornado caused extensive destruction in the city's downtown area; it was ultimately rated EF4. The final damage count was 867 residences and 94 businesses in Cullman; six people died as well.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-April_27,_2011,_Cullman,_Alabama_EF4_Tornado-49) The town of [Cordova, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordova,_Alabama "Cordova, Alabama"), which had already been damaged by an EF3 tornado from the initial round of storms, was struck by an EF4 tornado that killed 13 people. Two violent EF4 tornadoes also ripped through [Jackson County, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_County,_Alabama "Jackson County, Alabama"), one of which caused a fatality near [Bridgeport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridgeport,_Alabama "Bridgeport, Alabama") while the other passed near [Pisgah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pisgah,_Alabama "Pisgah, Alabama") and into Georgia where it caused major damage in [Trenton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trenton,_Georgia "Trenton, Georgia") and killed 14 people. At around 5:10 p.m. CDT (22:10 UTC), a very large and exceptionally destructive tornado struck [Tuscaloosa, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuscaloosa,_Alabama "Tuscaloosa, Alabama"), and about 40 minutes later, that same tornado struck the northern suburbs of nearby Birmingham.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-massive-50) A tornado emergency was issued for both cities, along with many other cities that day. Many local television stations, including WBRC and WBMA-LD/WCFT/WJSU, as well as [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS") affiliate [WIAT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WIAT "WIAT") (channel 42), broadcast live footage of this long-tracked tornado in both Tuscaloosa and Birmingham. A debris ball was observed by the Birmingham [NEXRAD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NEXRAD "NEXRAD"), indicating that the tornado was causing extreme damage.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-51) This tornado killed 64 people and caused extensive devastation in densely populated areas, and the tornado struck several of the same small communities as the [April 1956 F4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1956_Birmingham_tornado "April 1956 Birmingham tornado"), the [April 1977 F5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1977_Birmingham_tornado "April 1977 Birmingham tornado") and the [April 1998 F5 tornadoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Oak_Grove%E2%80%93Birmingham_tornado "1998 Oak Grove–Birmingham tornado") that hit portions of the Birmingham area. The supercell that produced the Tuscaloosa/Birmingham EF4 tornado originated in [Newton County, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton_County,_Mississippi "Newton County, Mississippi"). The same supercell produced another EF4 tornado later that evening that killed 22 people and struck the [Ohatchee, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohatchee,_Alabama "Ohatchee, Alabama"), area and eventually crossed into Georgia, causing additional damage near [Cave Spring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cave_Spring,_Georgia "Cave Spring, Georgia") before dissipating. Further to the south, a mile-wide EF3 tornado killed 7 people in mostly rural areas and caused major damage in the small town of [Eoline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eoline,_Alabama "Eoline, Alabama"). The final EF5 tornado of the day caused remarkable damage in and around the town of [Rainsville, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainsville,_Alabama "Rainsville, Alabama"), killing 25 people before crossing into Georgia and dissipating. Tornadoes continued touching down further to the northeast as the sun set, particularly in Georgia. This included a long-tracked EF4 tornado that caused major damage in [Ringgold, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ringgold,_Georgia "Ringgold, Georgia"), [Apison, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apison,_Tennessee "Apison, Tennessee"), and [Cleveland, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland,_Tennessee "Cleveland, Tennessee"), killing 20 people along the path. After dark, violent tornadoes continued to touch down, and a nighttime EF4 tornado destroyed many lakeside homes at [Lake Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Martin "Lake Martin") in eastern Alabama, killing seven people. Additional strong nighttime tornadoes occurred in Georgia, including an EF3 that killed two people in [Barnesville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnesville,_Georgia "Barnesville, Georgia"), and another EF3 that destroyed homes and killed one person at [Lake Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Burton_(Georgia) "Lake Burton (Georgia)").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-2011-super-outbreak-45)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-52)

#### Continued activity farther east

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2011_Super_Outbreak&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Continued activity farther east")]

Powerful tornadoes touched down across [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee") as well that evening. A violent EF4 struck the community of [New Harmony, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Harmony,_Tennessee "New Harmony, Tennessee"), where homes were leveled, vehicles were tossed, and four people were killed.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-53) On January 23, 2025, Anthony W. Lyza with the [National Severe Storms Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Severe_Storms_Laboratory "National Severe Storms Laboratory") along with Harold E. Brooks and Makenzie J. Kroca with the [University of Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oklahoma "University of Oklahoma")'s School of Meteorology published a paper to the [American Meteorological Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Meteorological_Society "American Meteorological Society"), where they stated the tornado in New Harmony was an "EF5 candidate". The paper was of the opinion that the EF5 starting wind speed should be 190 mph (310 km/h) instead of 201 mph (323 km/h).[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Lyza2025-54)

Two EF3 tornadoes crossed paths in [Greene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greene_County,_Tennessee "Greene County, Tennessee") and [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_County,_Tennessee "Washington County, Tennessee") counties (coming a couple of hours apart), resulting in eight fatalities. The rural communities of [Horse Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horse_Creek,_Tennessee "Horse Creek, Tennessee") and [Camp Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_Creek,_Tennessee "Camp Creek, Tennessee") suffered major damage from those tornadoes late that evening.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-55)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-56) A very large EF4 wedge tornado leveled a mile-wide swath of forest through 14 miles (23 km) of [Great Smoky Mountains National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Smoky_Mountains_National_Park "Great Smoky Mountains National Park"), resulting in many trails being closed.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-57)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-58) At [Chilhowee Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chilhowee_Dam "Chilhowee Dam"), large metal power line truss towers were torn and thrown from their concrete supports that they were anchored to.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-59)

A secondary area of severe weather also developed that afternoon and evening along a corridor extending from central and northern [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia "Virginia") northward through [Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland "Maryland"), [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania"), and [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"), continuing into early April 28. Many tornadoes touched down in this area as well.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-60)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-61) Most of these tornadoes were weak, though an EF2 tornado touched down near the town of [Halifax, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax,_Virginia "Halifax, Virginia"), and caused severe damage to homes in the area, resulting in one death.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-62) Tornado alerts were issued for [Southern Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Ontario "Southern Ontario") as far north as [Ottawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa "Ottawa") as well; one tornado was later confirmed in [Fergus, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fergus,_Ontario "Fergus, Ontario").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-63)

[![Image 372: SPC Storm Reports for 04/27/11 map updated at 12112 on 05/07/11, with tornado, wind, hail and total reports, high wind and large hail reports](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/SPC_Severe_weather_reports_20110427.png/250px-SPC_Severe_weather_reports_20110427.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SPC_Severe_weather_reports_20110427.png)

SPC Storm Reports for April 27

A statewide review by emergency management officials recorded 249 fatalities in Alabama as of the morning of April 30, 23 of which were not tornado-related.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-alemapressrelease1-14) Eventually, a total of 238 tornado-related deaths would be confirmed in the state. Damage and power outages in the [Huntsville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huntsville,_Alabama "Huntsville, Alabama") area were so widespread that at one point over 650,000 people were out of power in the [Tennessee Valley Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Valley_Authority "Tennessee Valley Authority") system. The EF5 tornado that struck Hackleburg and Phil Campbell damaged main high-transmission power lines coming from [Browns Ferry Nuclear Plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Browns_Ferry_Nuclear_Plant "Browns Ferry Nuclear Plant") near [Tanner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanner,_Alabama "Tanner, Alabama"). These towers were the main supply of electrical power to much of North Alabama, and some were without power for two weeks. The tornado just missed the Limestone Correctional Facility, which less than a year later would be struck by another tornado.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-64)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-65)

The Storm Prediction Center received 292 reports of tornadoes in the preceding 24 hours.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Storm_Reports_April_27-20) In addition to setting the record for most tornadoes in a calendar day (223; midnight to midnight CDT (05:00 – 05:00 [UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time "Coordinated Universal Time"))), it also broke the record for the most tornado touchdowns in any 24-hour period with 226 from 12:40 a.m. to 12:40 a.m. CDT (05:40 – 05:40 UTC) April 27–28, breaking the old 24-hour record of 148 set by the [1974 Super Outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_Super_Outbreak "1974 Super Outbreak"). Of those 226 tornadoes, 59 touched down in Alabama and 83 began in Tennessee, accounting for 62.8 percent of the tornadoes that touched down on April 27.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-66) On April 27 alone, the National Weather Service in Huntsville, Alabama, issued 92 tornado warnings, 31 [severe thunderstorm warnings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Severe_thunderstorm_warning "Severe thunderstorm warning"), and seven [flash flood warnings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flash_flood_warning "Flash flood warning").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-SWDJW-04272011-WarningSummaries-67)

Tornado watches were issued for the [Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean") coast from [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania") to [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida") at the start of the day and continued through the morning and early afternoon, but tornadoes were forecasted to generally be weaker and more isolated.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-68) Despite this, the secondary portion of the outbreak that had begun producing scattered tornadoes throughout the [Mid-Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-Atlantic_states "Mid-Atlantic states") and [East Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Coast_of_the_United_States "East Coast of the United States") regions the previous evening intensified during the early morning, producing numerous tornadoes. A particularly active region, in which there were some strong tornadoes,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-69) was the [Interstate 81](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_81 "Interstate 81") corridor extending from southwest [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia "Virginia"),[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-washingtonpost1-70) northward through the [Shenandoah Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shenandoah_Valley "Shenandoah Valley")[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-71) and into [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania"),[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-72) and [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"). This included the deadly EF3 tornado that struck the town of [Glade Spring, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glade_Spring,_Virginia "Glade Spring, Virginia"), very early in the morning, where three people died.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-73) Tornadoes were also reported in [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"),[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-74)[Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"), [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina "South Carolina"),[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-75)[North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina"),[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-76) and [Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland "Maryland"). Most of these tornadoes were weak. Although tornado watches were issued, no tornadoes were spotted in [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey")[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-77) or [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.")[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-washingtonpost1-70) In the wake of the tornadoes and severe thunderstorms, widespread flooding hit the Midwest, South, and Eastern Seaboard, with extensive flood and flash flood warnings issued.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-78) The last tornadoes of the outbreak touched down that afternoon in eastern [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina"), which was hard hit in the [April 16 outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_April_14%E2%80%9316,_2011 "Tornado outbreak of April 14–16, 2011"), though the tornadoes that impacted the area this time around were weak.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-79) After spawning one final round of isolated non-tornadic thunderstorms across central Florida that night into April 29, the system finally moved out into the Atlantic Ocean, having caused a great deal of devastation on its 4-day trek throughout the central and eastern US.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-80)

A record 368 tornadoes touched down over the span of four days, 37 of which were EF3+ tornadoes. Four tornadoes were rated EF5 – behind only the [1974 Super Outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_Super_Outbreak "1974 Super Outbreak") (7 F5s). Several of the strong to violent tornadoes that formed were exceptionally long-tracked, with six tornadoes on April 27 tracking over 60 miles (97 km). Many tornadoes on the afternoon of April 27 were spawned from a collection of supercells that moved across Mississippi, Alabama, Tennessee, and Georgia.

This section is about the 2011 EF2 tornado. For the tornado that impacted similar areas in 2014, see [2014 Mayflower–Vilonia tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Mayflower%E2%80%93Vilonia_tornado "2014 Mayflower–Vilonia tornado").

The first tornado of the outbreak to cause more than one death was this long-tracked, high-end EF2 wedge tornado that struck the small town of [Vilonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vilonia,_Arkansas "Vilonia, Arkansas") in [Faulkner County, Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faulkner_County,_Arkansas "Faulkner County, Arkansas"), around 7:30 p.m. [CDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Time_Zone "Central Time Zone") (00:30 [UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time "Coordinated Universal Time")) on April 25.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-NWSLittleRockApril27-83) A [tornado warning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_warning "Tornado warning") was issued for the area roughly 30 minutes prior to the tornado's arrival, and the relatively low loss of life was attributed to this lead time.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-TheCabin426-84) A [tornado emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_emergency "Tornado emergency") was declared at 7:24 p.m. CDT (00:24 UTC) for the city shortly before the tornado struck.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-85) Four people were killed in the town and many more were injured. The tornado touched down northwest of [Ferndale](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ferndale,_Arkansas&action=edit&redlink=1 "Ferndale, Arkansas (page does not exist)") in [Pulaski County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Arkansas "Pulaski County, Arkansas") at 6:48 p.m. CDT (23:48 UTC), downing trees and transmission towers at EF1 intensity.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-86) It continued northeast of [Natural Steps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Steps,_Arkansas "Natural Steps, Arkansas"), severely damaging a small church and downing numerous trees, one of which landed on a house.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-87) The tornado continued to knock down trees as it passed near [Roland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roland,_Arkansas "Roland, Arkansas"), several of which landed on homes. The tornado reached EF2 strength as it crossed into Faulkner County and passed southeast of [Mayflower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayflower,_Arkansas "Mayflower, Arkansas"), downing numerous trees and power lines and damaging homes and outbuildings. Past Mayflower, it continued towards Vilonia and struck a mobile home park, where numerous mobile homes were destroyed and the four fatalities occurred. Two of the fatalities occurred when a couple attempted to take shelter in a cargo container, which was thrown 150 yards (140 m) and deposited near a pond. Several other people were injured in this area as well. The tornado maintained EF2 intensity as it moved directly through Vilonia, damaging numerous homes and businesses and flipping several semi-trucks. The [American Red Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Red_Cross "American Red Cross") indicated that approximately 34 site-built houses and 62 mobile homes were destroyed, 91 site-built homes and 41 mobile homes suffered major damage, 145 site-built houses and 43 mobile homes had minor damage, and 53 site-built houses and 38 mobile homes were affected in some other way in the Vilonia area.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-88) One of the mobile homes was picked up and flipped, and the home's two bathtubs were found over a hill about 40 yards (37 m) away. The lone occupant of the mobile home sustained major injuries.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-89) After moving through Vilonia, the tornado weakened to EF1 strength as it moved into [White County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_County,_Arkansas "White County, Arkansas") and passed west of [El Paso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Paso,_Arkansas "El Paso, Arkansas"), where trees were blown over onto houses (damaging several roofs), barns and outbuildings were destroyed, an [RV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recreational_vehicle "Recreational vehicle") and the trailer portion of a tractor-trailer were overturned, and hundreds of trees were downed. The tornado finally dissipated north of [Joy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy,_Arkansas "Joy, Arkansas") at 7:59 p.m. CDT (00:59 UTC), after having travelled just over 51 miles (82 km). At its widest point, the tornado was 1.64 miles (2.64 km) wide.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-TheCabin426-84)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-90) Following the tornado, 85 members of the [U.S. National Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Guard_of_the_United_States "National Guard of the United States") were deployed to assist in search and rescue, debris clearing, security and traffic control.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-91)

On April 27, 2014, three years and two days after this tornado, [a violent EF4 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Mayflower%E2%80%93Vilonia_tornado "2014 Mayflower–Vilonia tornado") touched down west of Ferndale and moved along almost the same path as this tornado, causing 16 fatalities and many injuries. However, it affected more of Mayflower than this tornado did and caused greater damage all along the path, especially in Vilonia, before lifting near El Paso.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-NWSLittleRockApril27Vilonia-92)

### Philadelphia–Kemper County, Mississippi

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2011_Super_Outbreak&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Philadelphia–Kemper County, Mississippi")]

This violent, fast moving and destructive tornado, which became the first EF5 tornado of the outbreak touched down near the city of [Philadelphia, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia,_Mississippi "Philadelphia, Mississippi"), on April 27. The tornado touched down at 2:30 p.m. CDT (19:30 UTC) and traveled for nearly 29 miles (47 km) through [Neshoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neshoba_County,_Mississippi "Neshoba County, Mississippi"), [Kemper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kemper_County,_Mississippi "Kemper County, Mississippi"), [Winston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_County,_Mississippi "Winston County, Mississippi"), and [Noxubee Counties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noxubee_County,_Mississippi "Noxubee County, Mississippi"), reaching a maximum width of a 1⁄2-mile (0.80 km).[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-93)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Philadelphia,_MS_EF5_Survey-94) The tornado killed three people, injured eight others, and caused $1.1 million in damage across its path.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Philadelphia,_MS_EF5_Survey-94)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-95)

The supercell thunderstorm that produced this tornado formed around 1:00 p.m. CDT south of [Jackson, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi "Jackson, Mississippi").[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-PhiladelphiaEF5_1-96) Traveling briskly to the northeast, it warranted a severe thunderstorm warning within 25 minutes and was deemed potentially tornadic by 1:36 p.m. CDT.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-PhiladelphiaEF5_1-96)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-97) A tornado finally touched down at 2:30 p.m. CDT just east of the [Philadelphia Municipal Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_Municipal_Airport "Philadelphia Municipal Airport"). It quickly intensified and began producing EF5 damage by 2:38 p.m. CDT; extreme ground scouring, up to 2 feet (0.61 m) deep in places, occurred in northeastern Neshoba County. After crossing into Kemper County, the tornado obliterated a mobile home, killing all three inside.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Philadelphia,_MS_EF5_Survey-94) It reached EF5 strength a second time near the Kemper–Winston county line where extreme ground scouring again took place and pavement was scoured.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Philadelphia,_MS_EF5_Survey-94)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-PhiladelphiaEF5_1-96) Extreme tree damage took place along the track and it ultimately dissipated at 3:00 p.m. CDT about 6 miles (9.7 km) north of [Mashulaville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mashulaville,_Mississippi "Mashulaville, Mississippi").[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Philadelphia,_MS_EF5_Survey-94)

This was the first tornado to cause F5/EF5 damage in [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi") since the [Candlestick Park tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_Candlestick_Park_tornado_outbreak#Candlestick_Park_tornado "1966 Candlestick Park tornado outbreak") on March 3, 1966. Additionally, the formation of the [Smithville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithville,_Mississippi "Smithville, Mississippi") tornado later that day marked the first time since statistics have been kept that two EF5 tornadoes have been recorded in Mississippi on the same day. Prior to this, the last confirmed EF5 tornado was the [Parkersburg, Iowa tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Parkersburg%E2%80%93New_Hartford_tornado "2008 Parkersburg–New Hartford tornado") on May 25, 2008.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Philadelphia,_MS_EF5_Survey-94)

Rated as a high-end EF4, this highly visible multiple-vortex tornado tracked directly through downtown Cullman.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Long_Track_Tornado_Hits_Cullman,_Alabama-98) The tornado touched down at 2:40 p.m. CDT (19:40 UTC) on April 27 and tracked a 47-mile (76 km) damage path through [Cullman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cullman_County,_Alabama "Cullman County, Alabama"), [Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_County,_Alabama "Morgan County, Alabama"), and [Marshall Counties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_County,_Alabama "Marshall County, Alabama"), causing six deaths.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-April_27,_2011,_Cullman,_Alabama_EF4_Tornado-49) The Cullman tornado first touched down on the north side of [Lewis Smith Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Smith_Lake "Lewis Smith Lake") and caused light structural damage near [Crane Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crane_Hill,_Alabama "Crane Hill, Alabama") before intensifying and tracking directly towards Cullman, snapping numerous trees and heavily damaging several homes. The tornado entered Cullman while being tracked and broadcast live via several tower cameras, including those operated by Birmingham [Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_Broadcasting_Company "Fox Broadcasting Company") affiliate [WBRC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WBRC "WBRC") (channel 6) and [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company "American Broadcasting Company") affiliate [WBMA-LD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WBMA-LD "WBMA-LD")/[WCFT-TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSES "WSES")/[WJSU-TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WGWW "WGWW") (channels 58, 33, and 40 - "_ABC 33/40_"), for several minutes.In all, a total of 867 residences and 94 businesses within the city of Cullman were damaged or destroyed.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Long_Track_Tornado_Hits_Cullman,_Alabama-98)

[![Image 376: Aftermath of a tornado, showing a concrete foundation surrounded by debris and damaged structures](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/High-end_EF4_damage_to_a_home_northwest_of_Arab%2C_Alabama.jpg/250px-High-end_EF4_damage_to_a_home_northwest_of_Arab%2C_Alabama.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:High-end_EF4_damage_to_a_home_northwest_of_Arab,_Alabama.jpg)

High-end EF4 damage to a home northwest of Arab, where five fatalities occurred.

The tornado then passed just north of [Fairview](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairview,_Alabama "Fairview, Alabama") at EF4 intensity, completely destroying homes and debarking numerous hardwood trees. Pieces of debris were found speared through vehicles in this area.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-April_27,_2011,_Cullman,_Alabama_EF4_Tornado-49) In [Ruth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth,_Alabama "Ruth, Alabama"), just north of [Arab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab,_Alabama "Arab, Alabama"), a large but poorly anchored brick home was swept completely away in this area, with the debris scattered 100 yards (91 m) from the foundation. Arab's power grid was completely crippled by the tornado's effects, and many roads in the area were obstructed by downed trees and power lines. The tornado damaged and destroyed several other homes, garages, and sheds north of [Union Grove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Grove,_Alabama "Union Grove, Alabama") before it crossed the [Tennessee River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_River "Tennessee River") just downstream of [Guntersville Dam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guntersville_Dam "Guntersville Dam"). It snapped numerous trees in a forested area before dissipating southeast of [New Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Hope,_Alabama "New Hope, Alabama").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-April_27,_2011,_Cullman,_Alabama_EF4_Tornado-49)

Widespread power outages occurred in the immediate aftermath of the tornado, which were largely centered in Cullman County.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Almost 200 power poles in and around Cullman were leveled, and 4,000 volunteers from the [Tennessee Valley Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Valley_Authority "Tennessee Valley Authority") helped to restore power, although some residents were still without power a week after the tornado.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-99) The State of Alabama gave $5,989,728 (2011 [USD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USD "USD")) to the City of Cullman to aid with recovery efforts, and a further $1,294,892 (2011 USD) to Cullman County.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-:4-100) A plan was also set in place by the [University of Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Alabama "University of Alabama") to help fund recovery efforts.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-101) Six people were killed by the tornado; five in Ruth and one in rural Cullman County.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-102) The five deaths in Ruth occurred when the tornado directly impacted a well-constructed home at EF4 intensity, leveling the building and killing all of the residents of the home; all were in the same family. The sixth death as a result of the tornado took place in Cullman County, in the tornado's early stages.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-:1-103)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-:0-104)[Storm chaser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_chasing "Storm chasing") Dan Whittaker, who was observing the tornado as it moved through Cullman near him, stated that "this is not like any tornado I've seen anywhere."[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-105)

### Hackleburg–Phil Campbell–Tanner–Harvest, Alabama

This devastating, long-tracked and violent EF5 wedge tornado was the deadliest of the outbreak. It first touched down in [Marion County, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion_County,_Alabama "Marion County, Alabama"), about 5 miles (8.0 km) west-southwest of [Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton,_Alabama "Hamilton, Alabama") around 3:00 p.m. CDT (21:00 UTC) on April 27, leaving massive damage along its track. The storm would eventually reach the [Hackleburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hackleburg,_Alabama "Hackleburg, Alabama") area, completely leveling many homes and businesses, including a large [Wrangler, Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrangler_(Jeans) "Wrangler (Jeans)") factory. Most of the structures in downtown Hackleburg were badly damaged and Hackleburg High School was destroyed. Well-built homes were wiped cleanly from their foundations, extensive wind-rowing of debris occurred, trees were completely debarked, and cars were thrown hundreds of yards. According to the [American Red Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Red_Cross "American Red Cross"), 75 percent of the town was destroyed.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-106) While initially rated as an EF3, the rating was increased to EF5 after further analysis of the damage, making it the first F5/EF5 tornado in Alabama since the [Birmingham tornado of April 8, 1998](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1998_Birmingham_tornado "April 1998 Birmingham tornado").[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Marion_survey-107)

[![Image 378: Weather radar map displaying a severe storm with areas of high intensity rainfall, indicating potentially hazardous weather conditions](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/2011_Hackleburg-Phil_Campbell_tornado_radar_KGWX_2011-04-27_2033Z.png/250px-2011_Hackleburg-Phil_Campbell_tornado_radar_KGWX_2011-04-27_2033Z.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2011_Hackleburg-Phil_Campbell_tornado_radar_KGWX_2011-04-27_2033Z.png)

Radar image of the tornado as it neared the town of [Phil Campbell, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Campbell,_Alabama "Phil Campbell, Alabama"), with a [debris ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debris_ball "Debris ball") evident

Soon after crossing into [Franklin County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_County,_Alabama "Franklin County, Alabama"), the town of [Phil Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Campbell,_Alabama "Phil Campbell, Alabama") experienced significant devastation of the same magnitude as Hackleburg. Numerous homes, some of which were well-constructed, were swept away as the tornado tore through town. At least three churches along the path sustained significant damage, with one church in the town being completely destroyed and having only the foundation slab remaining. Mobile homes throughout the path were completely destroyed, and their mangled frames were tossed at least 25 to 50 yards (23 to 46 m). Cars were tossed and destroyed throughout the path of the tornado, with one car wrapped around a debarked tree. A 25-foot (7.6 m) section of pavement was torn from a road in this area as well. The most intense damage along the path occurred northeast of Phil Campbell in the rural community of Oak Grove, where vehicles were carried long distances and mangled beyond recognition, large trees were completely debarked, and large brick homes with extensive anchoring were obliterated with the debris wind-rowed hundreds of yards away. The tornado continued into [Lawrence County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_County,_Alabama "Lawrence County, Alabama"), impacting the [Mount Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Hope,_Lawrence_County,_Alabama "Mount Hope, Lawrence County, Alabama") community, where significant devastation was incurred to single-family homes and a restaurant. Nothing but the foundation and a pile of debris remained at the restaurant site, and a small portion of the restaurant's foundation slab buckled.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Huntsville_EF5-108)

[![Image 379: Extensive damage from a natural disaster, with debris scattered across the landscape and two cars visible among the wreckage](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/Toney2011.jpg/250px-Toney2011.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Toney2011.jpg)

A destroyed neighborhood in Toney, Alabama.

The tornado moved northeast, producing EF3 damage in and around [Langtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Langtown,_Alabama&action=edit&redlink=1 "Langtown, Alabama (page does not exist)"). The tornado re-intensified to EF4 strength as it passed near [Moulton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moulton,_Alabama "Moulton, Alabama") and [Trinity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity,_Alabama "Trinity, Alabama"), debarking trees, mangling, and leveling homes. It then continued through the northwest corner of [Morgan County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_County,_Alabama "Morgan County, Alabama"), crossed Wheeler Lake, and moved into [Limestone County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limestone_County,_Alabama "Limestone County, Alabama"), coming within 2 miles (3.2 km) of [Browns Ferry Nuclear Power Plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Browns_Ferry_Nuclear_Power_Plant "Browns Ferry Nuclear Power Plant"). The tornado caused power outages in the area, and the plant had to be shut down. The tornado continued towards the small community of Tanner.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-NWS-HUN-SWS-04282141-109)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-TFP-nuke-110)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-HUN-132.1mi-111)[Tanner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanner,_Alabama "Tanner, Alabama") experienced a large swath of EF4 damage and a narrow corridor of "high-end EF4 to near-EF5 damage". The storm "completely wiped clean" several well constructed homes with anchor bolting.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-NWS-HUN-SWS-04282141-109) As the storm crossed [US 72](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_72 "U.S. Route 72") in eastern Limestone County, the tornado destroyed a [Doppler radar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doppler_weather_radar "Doppler weather radar") operated by Huntsville [NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC "NBC") affiliate [WAFF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WAFF_(TV) "WAFF (TV)") (channel 48) and continued into East Limestone, a heavily populated area of Limestone County where homes in subdivisions were damaged or destroyed at high-end EF3 strength. As the storm crossed into Madison County, it approached the densely populated suburban communities of [Harvest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvest,_Alabama "Harvest, Alabama") and [Toney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toney,_Alabama "Toney, Alabama"), where it either damaged or destroyed hundreds of homes, especially in the Anderson Hills and Carter's Gin subdivisions. Many homes were reduced to rubble, and the damage in this area was rated mainly EF3 with a small pocket of EF4 damage in Harvest. The tornado completely destroyed a [Piggly Wiggly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piggly_Wiggly "Piggly Wiggly") grocery store in Harvest and severely damaged a convenience store and local bank, which was shut down for months following the event.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-SWDJW-04272011ToneyHarvestDestruction-112) The storm progressed across Pulaski Pike in northwest Madison County, damaging many homes, and dissipated soon afterwards. In all, hundreds of homes received moderate to major damage along the path from Limestone to Madison County with many of these being total losses.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-NWS-HUN-SWS-04282141-109)

Initially, the tornado was thought to have continued into [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee"). However, updates to the [Damage Assessment Toolkit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damage_Assessment_Toolkit "Damage Assessment Toolkit") (DAT) and analysis by damage surveyors, including a 2022 re-analysis of the outbreak by the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Oceanic_and_Atmospheric_Administration "National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration") (NOAA) and [National Severe Storms Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Severe_Storms_Laboratory "National Severe Storms Laboratory") (NSSL), determined that the Hackleburg tornado lifted after Madison County and assessed the portion in Tennessee to be a separate EF3 tornado.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Damage_Viewer-113)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-2022Analysis-114)

In total, this tornado killed 71 people, all in Alabama.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-spc_fatal-3) This made it the deadliest single tornado ever to strike the state of Alabama as well as (at the time) the deadliest in the United States since the 1955 [Udall, Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Udall,_Kansas "Udall, Kansas"), tornado that killed 80 people.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-115)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-116) In addition to being the deadliest, this tornado also had one of the longest tracks of any tornado in the outbreak, with its path extending 102 miles (164 km) across Northern Alabama.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-2022Analysis-114)

In response to the damage in Phil Campbell, one of the hardest hit communities, writer [Phil Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Campbell_(writer) "Phil Campbell (writer)") organized a fundraising and relief effort composed of 20 people with the name Phil Campbell or variations thereof. They traveled to the community from places as far away as Australia to aid in the cleanup effort. Many of these people had planned to attend a convention in June 2011 to commemorate the 100th anniversary of the city's incorporation.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-117)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-118)

### Reform–Oakman–Cordova–Blountsville, Alabama

Reform–Oakman–Cordova–Blountsville, Alabama[![Image 380: A tornado hovers in the sky behind a red barn](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/a/ae/2011_Central_Alabama_Tornado_at_EF4_intensity.webp/330px-2011_Central_Alabama_Tornado_at_EF4_intensity.webp.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2011_Central_Alabama_Tornado_at_EF4_intensity.webp)
The tornado at peak intensity moving over rural areas.
Meteorological history
Formed April 27, 2011, 3:40 p.m. [CDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Daylight_Time "Central Daylight Time") ([UTC−05:00](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC%E2%88%9205:00 "UTC−05:00"))

This violent and extremely long-tracked EF4 tornado touched down at 3:40 p.m. CDT (20:40 UTC) in northeastern [Pickens County, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pickens_County,_Alabama "Pickens County, Alabama"), where it strengthened while impacting structures at EF0 and EF1 intensity, moving past several smaller towns.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Cordova_tornado-119) As the tornado moved into [Cordova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordova,_Alabama "Cordova, Alabama") it reached EF3 intensity and heavily damaged the town. The tornado continued to strengthen as it moved across Alabama, reaching EF4 intensity as it passed northwest of [Sumiton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumiton,_Alabama "Sumiton, Alabama"). The tornado retained this intensity as it caused sporadic damage across rural Alabama, destroying numerous homes and debarking trees. It dissipated south of [Red Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Hill,_Alabama "Red Hill, Alabama"), lifted south-southwest of [Guntersville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guntersville,_Alabama "Guntersville, Alabama") at 5:56 p.m. CDT (22:56 UTC). Thousands of trees were downed along the tornado's path.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Marshall_County_survey-121) This tornado was on the ground for two hours and sixteen minutes, tracking for 127.8 miles (205.7 km) across seven counties making it the longest track tornado of the outbreak. It was rated as a low-end EF4 with winds of 170 mph (270 km/h). In total, 13 people were killed and 54 others were injured.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Cordova_tornado-119)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Marshall_County_survey-121)

Cordova was devastated by the tornado, which was the second major tornado to hit the community on April 27.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-122)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-123) Several businesses and other buildings were destroyed or heavily damaged in and outside of the town, and four were killed in the downtown area.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The city of Cordova was awarded $5,098,515 equivalent to $7,127,000 in 2024 to aid with recovery efforts after the tornado; Blount County was awarded $758,572 (equivalent to $1,060,000 in 2024).[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-:4-100) Recovery efforts continued for months after the tornadoes.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-124) In the weeks and months after the tornado, numerous fires started in downtown Cordova within the rubble, which further damaged structures and temporarily stunted recovery efforts.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-125)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-126)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-127)

### Smithville, Mississippi/Shottsville, Alabama

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2011_Super_Outbreak&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Smithville, Mississippi/Shottsville, Alabama")]

Smithville, Mississippi/Shottsville, Alabama[![Image 381: An outdoor scene shows a tornado touching down, with trees and land visible in the foreground](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/d/d5/2011_smithville_tornado.png/330px-2011_smithville_tornado.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2011_smithville_tornado.png)
The tornado at maximum intensity while impacting the east side of Smithville.
Meteorological history
Formed April 27, 2011, 3:42 p.m. [CDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Daylight_Time "Central Daylight Time") ([UTC−05:00](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC%E2%88%9205:00 "UTC−05:00"))
Dissipated April 27, 2011, 4:23 p.m. CDT (UTC−05:00)
Duration 41 minutes
EF5 tornado
_on the [Enhanced Fujita scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced\_Fujita\_scale "Enhanced Fujita scale")_

Overall effects

This extraordinarily violent and fast moving EF5 wedge tornado, with estimated winds of up to 205 mph (330 km/h), struck the town of [Smithville, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithville,_Mississippi "Smithville, Mississippi"), at 3:47 p.m. CDT (20:47 UTC) on April 27, resulting in catastrophic damage and numerous fatalities.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-NWSMemphisSmithvilleEF5-128) The tornado began 3 miles (4.8 km) west-southwest of Smithville along the [Tennessee–Tombigbee Waterway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee%E2%80%93Tombigbee_Waterway "Tennessee–Tombigbee Waterway") near the [Glover Wilkins Lock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glover_Wilkins_Lock "Glover Wilkins Lock") at 3:42 p.m. CDT (20:42 UTC), snapping numerous trees near the Smithville Recreation Area. The tornado then rapidly intensified as it approached town, reaching EF5 intensity. As the storm crossed Davis Road South, the ground was deeply scoured in a nearby field.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Smith._Damage_Imagery-129) The tornado swept away numerous homes and structures as it moved northeast, following [Highway 25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Highway_25 "Mississippi Highway 25"). A semi-truck was thrown a considerable distance and destroyed in this area, and at one residence that was swept away, part of the concrete foundation slab was pulled up and dislodged slightly.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-NWSMemphisSmithvilleEF5-128)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Smith._Damage_Imagery-129) Multiple well-anchored brick homes were completely swept away, and a large brick funeral home was reduced to a bare slab as the tornado exited at the northeast side of town, with the debris scattered and wind-rowed into an adjacent wooded area. Nearby granite tombstones were blown over in the opposite direction of the tornado's passage. Overall, the tornado destroyed 117 structures in Smithville and damaged 50 others, killing 16 people.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Smithville_NCDC-130) The tornado weakened as it continued through rural areas northeast of town and moved into [Itawamba County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Itawamba_County,_Mississippi "Itawamba County, Mississippi"), where it downed numerous trees and power lines and caused roof damage to a house before exiting the county.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Smith._Damage_Imagery-129)[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-131)

[![Image 382: Two images showing weather radar with greens and blues to the left and yellows and reds to the right](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Smithville_Tornado_Radar.png/250px-Smithville_Tornado_Radar.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Smithville_Tornado_Radar.png)

Radar image showing the supercell and [hook echo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hook_echo "Hook echo") of the storm that produced the Smithville tornado.

The tornado continued across the [Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama "Alabama") state line into [Marion County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion_County,_Alabama "Marion County, Alabama"), where it caused EF1-strength damage near [Bexar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bexar,_Alabama "Bexar, Alabama"). Continuing northeast, the tornado re-intensified as it struck the rural community of [Shottsville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shottsville,_Alabama "Shottsville, Alabama") at high-end EF3 intensity, where homes and mobile homes were destroyed and seven people were killed, and it produced additional high-end EF3 damage as it continued north of [Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton,_Alabama "Hamilton, Alabama").[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-auto-132) More structures were impacted as the tornado approached and crossed into [Franklin County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_County,_Alabama "Franklin County, Alabama"). The tornado then dissipated near the town of [Hodges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hodges,_Alabama "Hodges, Alabama") at 4:23 p.m. CDT (21:23 UTC). The damage path was 37.3 miles (60.0 km) long and 3⁄4 mile (1.2 km) wide at its widest point, and it killed a total of 23 people along its path. 137 other people were injured.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-auto-132)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-133)

### Pisgah–Flat Rock–Higdon, Alabama/Trenton, Georgia

Pisgah–Flat Rock–Higdon, Alabama/Trenton, Georgia[![Image 383: An aerial view showing houses and buildings with blue tarps covering the roofs](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Aerial_of_Trenton%2C_Georgia_following_an_EF4_tornado_on_April_27%2C_2011.png/330px-Aerial_of_Trenton%2C_Georgia_following_an_EF4_tornado_on_April_27%2C_2011.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Aerial_of_Trenton,_Georgia_following_an_EF4_tornado_on_April_27,_2011.png)
An aerial view of the damage in Trenton, Georgia by the tornado.
Meteorological history
Formed April 27, 2011, 4:01 p.m. [CDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Daylight_Time "Central Daylight Time") ([UTC−05:00](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC%E2%88%9205:00 "UTC−05:00"))
Dissipated April 27, 2011, 4:57 p.m. CDT (UTC−05:00)

EF4 tornado
_on the [Enhanced Fujita scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced\_Fujita\_scale "Enhanced Fujita scale")_

This multiple-vortex EF4 tornado that originated from the Cullman supercell, with maximum sustained winds of up to 190 mph (310 km/h), devastated portions of [Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_County,_Alabama "Jackson County, Alabama") and [DeKalb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DeKalb_County,_Alabama "DeKalb County, Alabama") counties in Alabama, as well as [Dade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dade_County,_Georgia "Dade County, Georgia") and [Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walker_County,_Georgia "Walker County, Georgia") counties in Georgia along a 47-mile-long (76 km) path at times up to 1,260 yards (1,150 m) wide, killing 14 people and injuring at least 50 others.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-NOAA-134)[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Storm_Events_Database-135)[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-ncdc.noaa.gov-136)

The tornado touched down north of [Section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Section,_Alabama "Section, Alabama"), initially producing EF0 to EF1 tree damage. The tornado rapidly intensified to low-end EF4 strength as it passed northwest of [Pisgah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pisgah,_Alabama "Pisgah, Alabama") and [Rosalie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosalie,_Alabama "Rosalie, Alabama"), destroying numerous mobile homes and block foundation homes, scattering the debris hundreds of yards and killing three people. Thousands of trees were snapped and debarked, vehicles were thrown up to 50 yards (46 m) in different directions, and barns and chicken houses were heavily damaged, along with the roof of a church.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-NOAA-134) As it passed near [Flat Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flat_Rock,_Alabama "Flat Rock, Alabama") and [Higdon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higdon,_Alabama "Higdon, Alabama"), the tornado reached high-end EF4 strength, mowing down thousands of trees in this rural area. The tornado later crossed into Georgia and crossed [Interstate 59](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_59 "Interstate 59") as it struck [Trenton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trenton,_Georgia "Trenton, Georgia") at EF3 intensity, killing two people. Dozens of homes in Trenton were either completely destroyed or sustained major damage, and tens of thousands of trees were downed in the area. A grocery store, two apartment complexes, and a funeral home were destroyed as well.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-Storm_Events_Database-135)

The tornado weakened to EF2 strength as it struck [Flintstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flintstone,_Georgia "Flintstone, Georgia") further to the northeast, but still resulted in major damage. Numerous trees and power lines were downed, 7 homes were destroyed, 26 sustained major damage, and 35 sustained minor damage in the Flintstone area. The tornado continued northeast, weakening to EF0 strength before finally dissipating near [Fort Oglethorpe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Oglethorpe,_Georgia "Fort Oglethorpe, Georgia").[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-ncdc.noaa.gov-136)

### Tuscaloosa–Birmingham, Alabama

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2011_Super_Outbreak&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Tuscaloosa–Birmingham, Alabama")]

Tuscaloosa–Birmingham, Alabama[![Image 384: Aerial view of a destroyed building complex and debris scattered around](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/Tuscaloosa_Apartment_Complex.JPG/330px-Tuscaloosa_Apartment_Complex.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tuscaloosa_Apartment_Complex.JPG)
The Tuscaloosa apartment complex was destroyed by the tornado.
Meteorological history
Formed April 27, 2011, 4:43 p.m. [CDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Daylight_Time "Central Daylight Time") ([UTC−05:00](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC%E2%88%9205:00 "UTC−05:00"))
Dissipated April 27, 2011, 6:14 p.m. CDT (UTC−05:00)
Duration 1 hour, 31 minutes
EF4 tornado
_on the [Enhanced Fujita scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced\_Fujita\_scale "Enhanced Fujita scale")_
Highest winds 190 mph (310 km/h)
Overall effects
